content: Pressure ulcers, also known as pressure sores or bedsores, are localized injuries to the skin and/or underlying tissue that occur due to prolonged pressure, often over bony areas of the body. These wounds are challenging to heal, cause significant pain, are costly to manage, and negatively affect patients' quality of life. Preventative measures include nutritional support, pressure redistribution, and the use of dressings or topical agents. However, the effectiveness of these dressings and agents in preventing pressure ulcers remains uncertain. This review aimed to evaluate the impact of these interventions on preventing pressure ulcers in individuals at risk, regardless of age or healthcare setting. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the use of dressings and topical agents for pressure ulcer prevention. A total of 18 trials involving 3,629 participants were analyzed. Nine trials focused on dressings, eight on topical agents, and one on both. The primary outcome measured was the incidence of pressure ulcers. Topical Agents: 1. Fatty Acid-Based Interventions: Two trials compared fatty acid-based treatments to olive oil. The pooled evidence did not show a clear difference in pressure ulcer incidence between the two groups (low-certainty evidence due to serious imprecision). Two trials compared fatty acid-based treatments to standard care. Again, no clear difference in pressure ulcer incidence was observed (low-certainty evidence due to risk of bias and imprecision). One trial reported that fatty acid-based treatments reduced pressure ulcer incidence compared to a control compound containing trisostearin and perfume (low-certainty evidence due to risk of bias and imprecision). Adverse events were not significantly different between fatty acid-based treatments and olive oil (low-certainty evidence due to very serious imprecision). 2. Other Topical Agents: Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) cream was associated with an increased risk of pressure ulcer development compared to placebo in one trial (low-certainty evidence due to risk of bias and imprecision). Three trials comparing other active topical agents (e.g., active lotion, Conotrane, Prevasore) to placebo or control showed no clear difference in pressure ulcer incidence (very low-certainty evidence due to serious risk of bias and imprecision). One trial suggested limited evidence that Dermalex™ might delay or prevent pressure ulcer development, but the findings were inconclusive (very low-certainty evidence due to serious risk of bias and imprecision). Adverse reactions were rare but slightly more frequent in the Dermalex™ group. Dressings: 1. Silicone Dressings: Six trials compared silicone dressings to no dressing. Silicone dressings may reduce the incidence of pressure ulcers (low-certainty evidence due to very serious risk of bias). In one trial with a low risk of bias, no clear difference in pressure ulcer incidence was observed between silicone dressings and placebo-treated groups (low-certainty evidence due to imprecision). 2. Other Dressings: One trial compared thin polyurethane dressings to no dressing and found no clear difference in pressure ulcer incidence (low-certainty evidence). The same trial reported a higher incidence of pressure ulcers with adhesive foam dressings compared to no dressing (very low-certainty evidence due to risk of bias and imprecision). Four trials compared other dressings (e.g., polyurethane film, hydrocolloid dressing, Kang’huier dressing, and a pressure ulcer preventive dressing) to various controls. No clear differences in pressure ulcer incidence were observed in most comparisons (very low-certainty evidence due to serious or very serious risk of bias and imprecision). Authors' Conclusions: The majority of trials investigating topical agents did not demonstrate clear benefits or harms in preventing pressure ulcers. Fatty acid-based treatments may reduce pressure ulcer incidence compared to certain control compounds, but the evidence is of low certainty. Silicone dressings may also reduce pressure ulcer incidence, but the certainty of evidence is low. Overall, the findings highlight the need for further high-quality research to confirm these results and provide more definitive guidance on the use of dressings and topical agents for pressure ulcer prevention.
